lessons.title: Lesson 1: Sourcing and Testing the 33 Ingredients Locally
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 7, Lesson 1. In this lesson we focus on the practical business of sourcing and testing the 33 ingredients that make up our organic manure. The first rule of this business is simple: your ingredients must come from within your own region, because transport costs will eat your profit faster than anything else. In Africa, we have an abundance of materials that most farmers and agripreneurs ignore. The 33 ingredients fall into five broad groups: animal manures, crop residues, kitchen and market waste, mineral and ash materials, and microbial boosters. Your job is to map what is available within a 30 kilometre radius of your production site. Start with animal manures. Cattle, goat, sheep, poultry, rabbit, and pig manure are the backbone. Poultry manure is high in nitrogen and phosphorus but must be composted well because it burns plants when fresh. Cattle and goat manure are balanced and safe. Rabbit manure is a hidden goldmine because it can be applied almost fresh. Next, crop residues. Maize stalks, rice husks, groundnut shells, banana pseudostems, coffee husks, cocoa pods, sugarcane bagasse, and coconut coir are all excellent carbon sources. Do not burn them. They are money. Kitchen and market waste includes vegetable peels, fruit waste, fish bones, eggshells, and spoiled produce from local markets. This is often free if you build relationships with market chairmen. Mineral and ash materials include wood ash, charcoal dust, limestone, rock phosphate, gypsum, and termite mound soil. These add calcium, potassium, phosphorus, and sulphur. Microbial boosters include effective microorganisms, molasses, milk, yeast, and healthy forest soil. These accelerate decomposition and improve the final product. Now, testing. You do not need a laboratory to start. Use your senses. Smell the material. A good ingredient smells earthy, not rotten or chemical. Feel it. It should crumble, not clump like wet clay. Look at the colour. Dark brown to black is good. Do a simple jar test for soil texture and a vinegar test for lime content. For serious commercial production, send samples to a government agricultural research station or a private lab. In Kenya, Uganda, Nigeria, Ghana, and South Africa, there are affordable soil and compost testing services. Test for pH, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, organic carbon, and moisture. Keep records. Every batch of ingredients should be logged with date, source, quantity, and test result. This record becomes your quality control and your marketing story. When you approach a buyer, you can show them exactly what went into the manure and why it works. Pricing is critical. Negotiate long-term contracts with poultry farms, cattle kraals, and markets. Offer to clean their pens or remove their waste for free or at a small fee. This turns a waste disposal problem into your raw material supply. In many African cities, market waste is a headache for authorities. You can become the solution and get paid twice: once for removing waste, and again for selling manure. Transport is the biggest hidden cost. Use locally made carts, bicycles, or shared trucks. Dry your ingredients before transport to reduce weight. A tonne of wet manure is mostly water. Sun-drying on a concrete slab or black plastic sheet can cut weight by half. That is money saved. Storage matters. Keep ingredients under a roof or tarp. Moisture causes nutrient loss and flies. Separate carbon-rich and nitrogen-rich materials. Never mix fresh manure with ash directly, because ammonia is lost. Build a simple shed with locally available poles, thatch, and plastic. Finally, think like a business from day one. Your sourcing plan should be written. List each of the 33 ingredients, the source, the monthly quantity, the cost, and the transport method. If an ingredient is not available, substitute it. The 33 ingredients are a guide, not a prison. The goal is a balanced, nutrient-rich, microbially active manure that improves soil and increases yields. In the next lesson, we will look at the exact ratios and the composting process. For now, go out and map your local supply chain. Talk to farmers, market traders, and livestock keepers. Your first batch starts with relationships, not recipes.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The 33-Ingredient Recipe and Composting Process
lessons.body: In Lesson 2 we move from sourcing to the actual recipe and composting process. This is where science meets sweat. The 33 ingredients are not thrown together randomly. They are combined in a specific sequence and ratio to create a balanced organic manure that feeds the soil, not just the plant. The target is a carbon to nitrogen ratio of about 25 to 30 to 1. Too much carbon and the pile sits cold. Too much nitrogen and you lose ammonia gas and get a slimy, smelly mess. Your 33 ingredients already fall into carbon-rich and nitrogen-rich categories. Carbon-rich materials include maize stalks, rice husks, sawdust, banana pseudostems, coffee husks, cocoa pods, sugarcane bagasse, coconut coir, dry leaves, and paper waste. Nitrogen-rich materials include poultry manure, cattle manure, goat manure, pig manure, rabbit manure, fish waste, vegetable peels, fruit waste, grass clippings, and green weeds. Mineral and ash materials like wood ash, charcoal dust, limestone, rock phosphate, gypsum, and termite soil are added in smaller quantities, usually 5 to 10 percent of the total volume. Microbial boosters like molasses, yeast, milk, effective microorganisms, and forest soil are added as a liquid spray or thin layers. Now the recipe. For a standard 1 tonne batch, use approximately 400 kilogrammes of carbon-rich materials, 400 kilogrammes of nitrogen-rich manures, 100 kilogrammes of mineral and ash materials, 50 kilogrammes of kitchen and market waste, and 50 kilogrammes of microbial boosters and water. This is a guide. Adjust based on what you have. The key is to chop everything small. Particle size should be 2 to 5 centimetres. Smaller particles decompose faster. Use a machete, a chaff cutter, or a simple shredder. In many African villages, a group of youth with machetes can chop a tonne in a few hours. That is employment. Build your pile in layers. Start with a 15 centimetre layer of coarse carbon material like maize stalks or rice husks. This allows air to enter from the bottom. Then add a 10 centimetre layer of nitrogen-rich manure. Then a thin layer of ash and minerals. Then a thin layer of kitchen waste. Then sprinkle microbial booster liquid. Repeat these layers until the pile is 1.5 to 2 metres high. Do not compact it. Keep it loose. Cover with banana leaves, grass, or a tarp to retain moisture and heat. Turn the pile every 3 to 5 days for the first three weeks. Turning introduces oxygen, mixes materials, and prevents anaerobic pockets. After three weeks, turn every 7 to 10 days. In total, composting takes 6 to 10 weeks depending on climate. In hot, dry areas, keep the pile moist like a wrung-out sponge. In wet areas, cover it to prevent waterlogging. Monitor temperature. A good pile heats up to 55 to 65 degrees Celsius within 3 days. This heat kills weed seeds and pathogens. If the pile does not heat up, it is too dry or lacks nitrogen. Add water or fresh manure. If it smells like rotten eggs, it is too wet or compacted. Turn it and add carbon material. If it smells like ammonia, you have too much nitrogen. Add carbon material. When is it ready? The pile shrinks to about one third of its original size. It stops heating. It smells earthy like forest soil. It is dark brown to black. Earthworms may appear. The original materials are no longer recognisable. That is finished compost. Now, quality control. Do a simple germination test. Take a handful of compost, mix with water, and soak bean or maize seeds. If they germinate and grow normally, the compost is mature. If they die or turn yellow, the compost is still immature or too salty. Do a pH test with litmus paper or a cheap meter. Most crops prefer pH 6 to 7.5. If too acidic, add wood ash or limestone. If too alkaline, add more carbon material or a little sulphur. Packaging and storage. Dry the compost to about 20 to 30 percent moisture. Sieve it to remove stones and large pieces. Package in 50 kilogramme woven bags or 5 kilogramme retail packs. Store in a dry, shaded place. Do not stack more than 10 bags high. Label with the batch number, date, and ingredient list. This traceability is your competitive advantage. Many farmers in Africa have been sold fake or poor-quality manure. You will be different. Your 33-ingredient manure will be consistent, tested, and trusted. In the next lesson, we will look at application rates for different crops and how to train farmers to use it correctly. Remember, the recipe is a living document. Keep records of every batch. Note what worked and what did not. Adjust. That is how you build a business that lasts.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Application Rates and Crop-Specific Use
lessons.body: Welcome to Lesson 3. You have sourced your 33 ingredients and produced high-quality compost. Now you must apply it correctly. The biggest mistake farmers make is using too little or too much. Too little and they see no difference. Too much and they waste money and may burn plants. This lesson gives you practical application rates for major African crops. First, understand that organic manure is not a direct replacement for synthetic fertiliser in terms of immediate nutrient release. It is a soil conditioner and a slow-release nutrient bank. It improves soil structure, water holding capacity, and microbial life. Over time, it reduces the need for synthetic inputs. But in the first season, you may need to combine it with a small amount of starter fertiliser if your soil is severely depleted. The general rule is 2 to 4 tonnes of finished compost per hectare for cereals like maize, sorghum, millet, and rice. That is 200 to 400 grammes per planting hill if you are planting in stations. For maize, apply 200 to 300 grammes per hill at planting, mixed with the soil. Do not place seed directly on fresh compost. Let it sit for a week or plant beside it. For vegetables like tomatoes, peppers, onions, and cabbage, use 4 to 6 tonnes per hectare. That is about 400 to 600 grammes per plant. Apply half at transplanting and half four weeks later as a side dress. For leafy vegetables like kale, spinach, and amaranth, use 3 to 5 tonnes per hectare. Apply before planting and top dress after every harvest. For root crops like carrots, beetroot, and radish, use 3 to 4 tonnes per hectare. Too much nitrogen from fresh manure causes forking and hairy roots. Use well-matured compost. For tubers like potatoes, sweet potatoes, and cassava, use 4 to 5 tonnes per hectare. Apply in the planting furrow and cover with soil. For legumes like beans, cowpeas, groundnuts, and soybeans, use 1 to 2 tonnes per hectare. Legumes fix their own nitrogen, so they need less. But they respond well to phosphorus and potassium from ash and rock phosphate in your compost. For fruit trees like mango, avocado, citrus, and banana, apply 5 to 10 kilogrammes per tree per year, split into two applications. Spread around the drip line, not against the trunk. For banana, apply 2 to 3 kilogrammes per mat every three months. For coffee and tea, apply 2 to 4 kilogrammes per bush per year. For pasture and fodder crops like napier grass, Rhodes grass, and lucerne, use 5 to 8 tonnes per hectare per year, split into three or four applications. Now, application methods. Broadcasting is the cheapest but wastes material. Banding along planting rows is better. Spot application in planting holes is best for expensive compost. Mix compost with soil to avoid concentration. Water immediately after application. Do not apply during heavy rain because nutrients leach away. Do not apply on dry, cracked soil because it will not incorporate. For liquid manure, which you can make by soaking your compost in water for 24 to 48 hours, use a dilution of 1 part compost to 10 parts water. Apply as a foliar spray or soil drench every two weeks. This is excellent for vegetables and young seedlings. Now, training farmers. Your business is not just selling manure. It is selling knowledge. Offer a simple one-page application guide with every bag. Use pictures and local language. Train farmers in groups of 20 to 30. Show them a demonstration plot. Let them see the difference between compost-treated and untreated crops. This builds trust and repeat sales. Pricing. Your manure should be priced competitively with synthetic fertiliser but not too cheap. In many African countries, a 50 kilogramme bag of NPK costs between 30 and 50 US dollars. Your 50 kilogramme bag of 33-ingredient compost can sell for 15 to 25 US dollars, depending on the market. But remember, compost is bulkier. You need to sell more bags per hectare. That is why you must also sell the knowledge. When a farmer understands that compost improves their soil for years, they will buy every season. Record keeping. Keep a simple notebook or phone app. Record the farmer name, crop, area, amount sold, and date. Follow up after one month and after harvest. Ask for feedback. Take photos. Use these as testimonials in your marketing. In the next lesson, we will look at business models, pricing, and distribution. But first, master application. A farmer who uses your manure correctly will become your best salesperson. A farmer who uses it wrongly will blame your product. So invest time in training. It pays.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Business Models, Pricing, and Distribution
lessons.body: Lesson 4 is about turning your 33-ingredient manure into a profitable business. Many people can make compost. Few can make money from it. The difference is business discipline. Start with your cost structure. Calculate the cost of every ingredient, even if it is free. Free materials still cost labour, transport, and storage. For a 1 tonne batch, list all costs: raw materials, labour for collection and chopping, water, microbial boosters, packaging, transport, and marketing. Add 20 percent for overheads and 20 percent for profit. That gives you your selling price. For example, if your total cost per 50 kilogramme bag is 8 US dollars, your selling price should be at least 12 to 14 US dollars. Do not undercut yourself. There is no future in selling at cost. Now, business models. Model one is direct retail. You sell bags to individual farmers at markets, agro-dealer shops, or from your production site. This gives the highest price per bag but requires you to handle many small transactions. Model two is wholesale. You sell in bulk to agro-dealers, cooperatives, or NGOs. The price per bag is lower, but you move volume quickly. Model three is contract farming. You sign an agreement with a commercial farm, plantation, or greenhouse to supply a fixed quantity every month. This gives you predictable income and allows you to plan production. Model four is training and consultancy. You sell your manure together with training on how to use it. This can be a package: 10 bags plus a half-day training for a group of farmers. Model five is franchising or licensing. You train other youth groups or women groups to produce the same 33-ingredient manure under your brand. You earn a licence fee or a percentage of sales. This is how you scale without owning everything. Model six is waste management contracts. You get paid by municipalities, markets, or large livestock farms to remove their waste. You then turn that waste into manure. You get paid twice. Now, pricing strategies. Use psychological pricing. Sell a 50 kilogramme bag for 19.99 instead of 20. Use bundle pricing. Sell 10 bags for the price of 9. Use seasonal pricing. Raise prices during planting season and offer discounts during off-season. Use credit wisely. Many farmers cannot pay cash. Offer a buy-now-pay-later arrangement with a small deposit and the balance after harvest. But only do this with farmers you trust or through a cooperative that guarantees payment. Distribution. Your manure is heavy and bulky. Distribution is your biggest challenge. Use decentralised production. Instead of one big factory, set up small production sites near raw materials and near markets. Use local transport: bicycles, motorcycles, tricycles, and donkey carts. Partner with agro-dealers who already have a distribution network. Give them a 20 to 30 percent margin. They will push your product. Use digital tools. WhatsApp groups, Facebook Marketplace, and local radio are powerful in Africa. Create a simple logo and brand name. Use a consistent bag design. Put your phone number on every bag. Offer free delivery for orders above a certain quantity. Now, marketing. Do not just say your manure is organic. Show results. Create demonstration plots at schools, churches, mosques, and community centres. Take before and after photos. Invite local leaders and journalists. Use testimonials from respected farmers. Run a competition for the best yield using your manure. Give a prize. This generates word-of-mouth. Partner with extension officers, NGOs, and government programmes. Many African governments subsidise fertiliser. Position your manure as a complementary product, not a competitor. It improves the efficiency of synthetic fertiliser. Now, financial management. Keep business money separate from personal money. Open a bank account or mobile money account. Record every sale and expense. Pay yourself a salary. Reinvest at least 30 percent of profit into equipment, storage, and marketing. Build a reserve for the dry season when sales are low. Insurance is rare in this sector, but you can self-insure by keeping a cash buffer. Finally, think about scaling. Start small. Produce 1 tonne per week. Master the process. Then double. Then double again. Do not borrow heavily to expand before you have a reliable market. Grow with your customers. In the next and final lesson, we will look at quality control, certification, and long-term sustainability. But remember, a business is not just about making money. It is about solving a problem. Your problem is soil degradation and expensive fertiliser. Your solution is 33-ingredient organic manure. Sell that solution.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Quality Control, Certification, and Scaling
lessons.body: Welcome to the final lesson of Module 7. You have learned to source, produce, apply, and sell your 33-ingredient organic manure. Now we focus on quality control, certification, and scaling. These are the pillars that turn a small project into a lasting enterprise. Quality control starts with standard operating procedures. Write down every step of your production process. How much of each ingredient? How long do you compost? How often do you turn? What is the target moisture? What is the target pH? Who is responsible for each step? Train your workers on these procedures. Use a checklist for every batch. Sign and date it. This is your proof of quality. Test every batch. At minimum, do a germination test and a smell test. Better, use a simple soil test kit to check pH, nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Best, send samples to a laboratory every three months. Keep a sample of each batch for at least six months. If a customer complains, you can test the retained sample. If there is a problem, you can trace it back to the ingredient or the process. This is how you build a reputation. Now, certification. In many African countries, organic certification is expensive and bureaucratic. But there are alternatives. Join a local organic farmers association. They often have group certification. This reduces cost. Follow the standards of the East African Organic Products Standard, the Nigerian Organic Agriculture Network, or the South African Organic Sector Organisation. Even if you do not get formal certification, you can use a self-declaration. Write a simple document that states your ingredients, your process, and your commitment to organic principles. Get it stamped by a local agricultural officer. This builds trust. For export markets, you will need formal certification. Start with a local certifier and work up. But do not let certification stop you from selling locally. Most African farmers care more about results than certificates. Show them results. Now, scaling. There are three ways to scale: volume, geography, and product range. Volume scaling means producing more of the same product. Invest in better equipment: a shredder, a mixer, a sieving machine, a weighing scale, and a bag sealer. These reduce labour and increase consistency. Geography scaling means setting up production sites in new areas. Use the franchise model from Lesson 4. Train local groups. Give them your recipe, your brand, and your quality standards. Buy back their product or let them sell under your brand for a fee. Product range scaling means creating new products from your manure. You can make liquid fertiliser, seed coating, potting mix, and soil blocks for nurseries. You can also blend your manure with biochar, rock phosphate, or beneficial microbes for specific crops. Each new product opens a new market. Now, sustainability. Your business depends on a steady supply of raw materials. Do not exhaust your sources. Work with farmers to integrate livestock and crop production. Encourage them to compost their own waste. You can buy surplus from them. Plant trees for biomass. Use agroforestry species like moringa, gliricidia, and leucaena. These provide nitrogen-rich leaves for your compost. Harvest water. Use rainwater harvesting to keep your compost moist. Use solar power for lighting and small machines. Reduce, reuse, and recycle your packaging. Offer a discount for returned bags. Now, risk management. What if a key ingredient becomes unavailable? Have substitutes ready. What if a disease kills your livestock? Diversify your sources. What if a customer claims your manure damaged their crop? Have a clear refund or replacement policy. Investigate the claim. If it is your fault, fix it. If it is not, explain politely. Never argue publicly. What if the government changes regulations? Join an industry association. Stay informed. What if the market price of synthetic fertiliser drops? Your organic manure still has value because it improves soil health. Emphasise that. Finally, think about legacy. Train your children, your workers, and your community. Write down your knowledge. Make videos. Hold workshops. The 33-ingredient organic manure is not just a product. It is a movement. It is a way to restore African soils, reduce dependence on imported fertiliser, create jobs, and improve food security. You are part of that movement. Your business can be profitable and principled. Start today. Measure everything. Improve every batch. Treat your customers like partners. And never stop learning. This concludes Module 7. You now have the knowledge to produce, apply, sell, and scale a 33-ingredient organic manure business. Go and build it.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Organic Manure with 33 Ingredients

This practical reference module consolidates the operational knowledge from Lessons 1â5 into a single field-ready guide for African agribusiness operators producing and selling 33-ingredient organic manure. Whether you are supplying smallholder maize growers in Kenya, vegetable producers in Ghana, or tea estates in Rwanda, the numbers, safety rules, and business benchmarks below are drawn from FAO, ILRI, WHO, and university extension data relevant to tropical and sub-Saharan African conditions.

Why the 33-Ingredient Approach Works in African Soils

Sub-Saharan African soils are among the most nutrient-depleted globally. FAO estimates that Africa loses about 30 kg of nutrients per hectare per year through erosion, leaching, and crop harvest â roughly 8 million tonnes annually across the continent. A single-ingredient manure rarely closes that gap. The 33-ingredient formula addresses this by combining:

  • Bulk carbon sources (maize stover, rice husks, sawdust, banana pseudostems) â feed the compost heap and build soil organic matter.
  • Nitrogen activators (poultry litter, goat droppings, urine-soaked bedding, legume haulms) â drive thermophilic decomposition.
  • Mineral and ash amendments (wood ash, bone meal, rock phosphate, dolomite, gypsum) â supply P, K, Ca, Mg, S.
  • Biological inoculants (forest topsoil, termite mound soil, effective microorganisms, aged manure slurry) â seed the heap with decomposer microbes.
  • Moisture and pH buffers (clay, charcoal dust, lime, fresh green matter) â stabilise the process.

For a commercial producer, the value proposition is straightforward: one bag of blended, cured manure replaces the need for the farmer to source five to ten separate inputs. That convenience margin is where your profit sits.

Business tip: Price your manure per tonne so that the cost per kg of N, P, and K is 20â40% below the local mineral fertiliser equivalent. This is the sweet spot where farmers switch and you still keep a healthy margin.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Pathogens, Ammonia, and Chemical Contamination

Organic manure is a biological and chemical hazard if mishandled. WHO and FAO jointly classify untreated animal manure as a Category 2 biological risk for human health, particularly for Salmonella, E. coli O157:H7, Cryptosporidium, and Ascaris eggs.

  • Never apply fresh (uncomposted) manure to vegetables eaten raw (lettuce, tomato, cucumber, herbs). WHO recommends a 60-day interval between manure application and harvest for crops in contact with soil, and 120 days for root crops.
  • Compost must reach 55â65Â°C for at least 3 consecutive days (turn the heap to ensure all material passes through the hot zone) to kill pathogens and weed seeds. Use a compost thermometer â do not guess.
  • Ammonia gas from poultry litter and urine-soaked bedding can cause respiratory damage. Work in well-ventilated areas, wear an N95 mask when turning heaps, and never enter a closed compost shed without ventilation.
  • Chemical contamination risk: manure from animals treated with antibiotics (especially from intensive poultry operations) can carry residues. Source from farms with a documented 14-day withdrawal period after medication. MSD Animal Health and Aviagen both publish withdrawal guidance.
  • Personal protective equipment (PPE): gloves, boots, long trousers, and eye protection when handling ash, lime, and rock phosphate dust. Wood ash is caustic â it can burn skin and eyes.
  • Do not mix manure with fresh chlorinated water â chlorine kills the beneficial microbes you are trying to cultivate.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Source locally and verify: Confirm at least 25 of the 33 ingredients are available within 50 km of your production site. Test pH and moisture of each bulk input before blending.
  2. Maintain C:N ratio between 25:1 and 35:1: Too much carbon (sawdust, rice husk) slows decomposition; too much nitrogen (poultry litter, urine) causes ammonia loss and odour.
  3. Target 50â60% moisture: The "squeeze test" â a handful should feel like a wrung-out sponge, with one or two drops released. Add water or dry material accordingly.
  4. Turn the heap 4â6 times over 6â8 weeks: Turn when core temperature drops below 50Â°C. This re-oxygenates and homogenises the batch.
  5. Test maturity before bagging: A cress seed germination test (â¥80% germination in manure extract vs. water control) confirms the compost is cured and not phytotoxic.
  6. Bag and label with batch number, date, NPK analysis, and application instructions: This is your legal and marketing differentiator. Buyers pay 15â30% more for labelled, analysed manure.
  7. Price per kg of N-P-K at 20â40% below mineral fertiliser equivalent: Use local DAP, CAN, and urea prices as your benchmark. Review quarterly.
  8. Keep a batch log: Record ingredient sources, dates, temperatures, turn dates, and lab results. This is required for certification (e.g., Kenya Organic Agriculture Network, Ghana Organic Agriculture Network) and protects you if a customer claims crop damage.

Business-First Notes for African Producers

The 33-ingredient manure business is a volume-and-trust business. Your margins come from three places:

  • Input cost arbitrage: Most ingredients are waste streams â maize stover, poultry litter, market vegetable waste, wood ash from bakeries and brick kilns. Negotiate free or low-cost collection agreements. A 10-tonne batch can be produced for US$150â400 in inputs in most East and West African markets.
  • Retail price: A 50 kg bag of quality organic manure retails for US$8â20 in Kenya, Ghana, and Nigeria (2024 prices). Production cost per bag is typically US$3â7. Gross margin: 40â60%.
  • Distribution leverage: Partner with agro-dealers, cooperatives, and county/national extension services. In Kenya, the Kenya Cereal Enhancement Programme and similar initiatives buy organic inputs in bulk for farmer groups â this is your fastest route to 10+ tonne monthly volumes.

Scale requires consistency. A farmer who buys your bag once and sees a 30% maize yield increase will buy again â and tell ten neighbours. A farmer who gets a bad batch will tell fifty. Quality control is not optional; it is your marketing budget.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Farmer's Compost Handbook: Experiences in Latin America (2015) â Practical composting methods, heap management, and quality indicators applicable to African conditions.
  • ILRI â Manure Management and Soil Fertility in Smallholder Systems (search "manure" in ILRI publications) â Research on manure quality, storage losses, and integrated soil fertility management in East Africa.
  • WHO â Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater, Excreta and Greywater in Agriculture (Vol. 4) â The global reference on pathogen reduction, waiting periods, and safe manure use in crop production.
  • University of Missouri Extension â Using Manure as Fertiliser â Clear nutrient tables, application calculations, and safety guidance transferable to African farm planning.
  • Aviagen â Broiler Litter Management and Nutrient Content Technical Resources â Poultry litter nutrient data and withdrawal-period guidance for sourcing safe manure from broiler operations.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of Module 7 in the Organic Manure with 33 Ingredients course?
options: A) To teach field application timing and dosage
B) To list the 33 ingredients only
C) To explain composting equipment brands
D) To replace soil testing entirely
quiz.explanation: Module 7 focuses on practical field application, including correct timing and dosage for best results.

quiz.q: Which factor most affects the decomposition rate of a 33 ingredient organic manure pile?
options: A) Color of the storage bin
B) Carbon to nitrogen ratio and moisture
C) Number of earthworms only
D) Price of raw materials
quiz.explanation: The carbon to nitrogen ratio, moisture, aeration, and temperature are key drivers of decomposition speed.

quiz.q: When applying organic manure with 33 ingredients, why should it be incorporated into the soil rather than left on the surface?
options: A) To make it look tidy
B) To increase its weight
C) To reduce nutrient loss and improve root contact
D) To prevent birds from eating it
quiz.explanation: Incorporation reduces volatilization and runoff losses and places nutrients closer to active roots.

quiz.q: What is a recommended safety practice when handling the 33 ingredient organic manure during mixing?
options: A) Work barefoot for better feel
B) Avoid all ventilation
C) Store it in drinking water containers
D) Wear gloves, mask, and eye protection
quiz.explanation: Personal protective equipment prevents skin, eye, and respiratory irritation from dust and microbes.

quiz.q: Which application method is best for row crops using finely sifted 33 ingredient organic manure?
options: A) Band placement near the seed row
B) Broadcasting over the entire field only
C) Foliar spraying of dry powder
D) Mixing with herbicide in the tank
quiz.explanation: Band placement concentrates nutrients near roots, improving efficiency and reducing waste.

quiz.q: How can a farmer tell that the 33 ingredient organic manure is fully matured and safe to use?
options: A) It smells strongly of ammonia
B) It is dark, crumbly, and earthy smelling
C) It is hot to the touch
D) It still contains visible food scraps
quiz.explanation: Mature compost is dark, crumbly, earthy smelling, and no longer heats up, indicating stable organic matter.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of applying immature 33 ingredient organic manure to crops?
options: A) It improves seed germination
B) It reduces weed pressure
C) It can burn plants and tie up nitrogen
D) It increases soil pH instantly
quiz.explanation: Immature manure can heat up, release ammonia, and cause microbial nitrogen immobilization, harming crops.

quiz.q: Which practice best preserves the nutrient value of 33 ingredient organic manure after application?
options: A) Leaving it exposed to direct sun and rain
B) Applying before heavy rain is forecast
C) Mixing it with fresh lime and storing wet
D) Applying at the right rate and irrigating lightly
quiz.explanation: Correct application rate and light irrigation help incorporate nutrients without causing runoff or leaching losses.

quiz.q: Which approach best helps a smallholder in Africa source the 33 ingredients locally?
options: A) Import all inputs from overseas suppliers
B) Map nearby farms, markets, and agro-waste streams
C) Buy only from one distant wholesaler
D) Wait for government to deliver all materials
quiz.explanation: Mapping local farms, markets, and agro-waste streams reduces cost and builds community supply chains.

quiz.q: Why is laboratory testing of local ingredients important before composting?
options: A) It increases the price of the final manure
B) It confirms nutrient levels and detects contaminants
C) It replaces the need for composting
D) It is required only for export crops
quiz.explanation: Testing reveals nutrient content, moisture, and possible toxins or heavy metals that affect safety and quality.

quiz.q: A farmer finds rice husks, poultry litter, and banana peels nearby. What should be done first?
options: A) Mix them immediately without checking
B) Record quantities, sources, and test key properties
C) Sell them raw at the market
D) Burn them to reduce volume
quiz.explanation: Recording and testing ensures the 33-ingredient recipe is consistent and safe before mixing.

quiz.q: Which local material is commonly used in African composting for carbon-rich bulk?
options: A) Fresh cattle urine
B) Maize cobs and straw
C) Plastic packaging
D) Diesel fuel
quiz.explanation: Maize cobs and straw are abundant carbon sources that balance nitrogen-rich materials.

quiz.q: What is a practical field test for moisture when preparing compost?
options: A) Squeeze test showing a few drops
B) Weighing with a laboratory balance
C) Measuring pH with a digital meter
D) Testing with a magnet
quiz.explanation: The squeeze test is a simple field method to check if compost has adequate moisture.

quiz.q: In the 33-ingredient recipe, why are ingredients grouped by function?
options: A) To make the recipe look complicated
B) To balance carbon, nitrogen, minerals, and microbes
C) To avoid using local materials
D) To increase transport costs
quiz.explanation: Grouping by function ensures nutrient balance and microbial activity during composting.

quiz.q: Which sequence is correct for the composting process?
options: A) Heap, water, cover, turn, cure
B) Cure, heap, sell, turn, water
C) Turn, cure, heap, water, cover
D) Water, sell, cover, heap, cure
quiz.explanation: Building the heap, watering, covering, regular turning, and curing are standard composting steps.

quiz.q: Why is turning the compost pile important?
options: A) It adds new ingredients automatically
B) It aerates the pile and speeds decomposition
C) It removes all nutrients
D) It makes the pile heavier
quiz.explanation: Turning supplies oxygen to microbes, controls temperature, and promotes even decomposition.

quiz.q: What temperature range indicates active thermophilic composting?
options: A) 5 to 10 degrees Celsius
B) 15 to 20 degrees Celsius
C) 45 to 65 degrees Celsius
D) 100 to 120 degrees Celsius
quiz.explanation: Thermophilic microbes thrive around 45 to 65 degrees Celsius, killing pathogens and weed seeds.

quiz.q: When is compost considered mature and ready for use?
options: A) When it smells like ammonia
B) When it is dark, crumbly, and earthy smelling
C) When it is still hot and steaming
D) When it contains visible food scraps
quiz.explanation: Mature compost is dark, crumbly, earthy, and cool, indicating stable organic matter.

quiz.q: For a cereal crop like maize, what is a typical application rate for organic manure?
options: A) 0 kilograms per hectare
B) 2 to 5 tonnes per hectare
C) 50 to 100 tonnes per hectare
D) 500 tonnes per hectare
quiz.explanation: Cereals generally respond well to 2 to 5 tonnes per hectare depending on soil fertility.

quiz.q: How should application rates differ for vegetables compared to cereals?
options: A) Vegetables usually need higher rates and more frequent applications
B) Vegetables need no manure at all
C) Vegetables need only chemical fertilizer
D) Vegetables need less than cereals always
quiz.explanation: Vegetables are heavy feeders and often require higher rates and split applications.

quiz.q: What is a good method to apply organic manure to tree crops?
options: A) Spray it on leaves only
B) Place it in a ring around the drip line
C) Bury it at the trunk base
D) Scatter it on the road
quiz.explanation: Applying manure around the drip line places nutrients where feeder roots can access them.

quiz.q: Why should farmers avoid applying fresh manure directly to crops?
options: A) It is too dry
B) It can burn plants and carry pathogens
C) It has no nutrients
D) It is illegal everywhere
quiz.explanation: Fresh manure can burn roots and introduce harmful pathogens; composting stabilizes it.

quiz.q: Which business model helps a compost producer reach many smallholder farmers?
options: A) Selling only to one large estate
B) Working through farmer cooperatives and agro-dealers
C) Giving away all manure for free
D) Exporting all manure overseas
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives and agro-dealers provide distribution networks to reach many smallholders.

quiz.q: What is a fair pricing strategy for organic manure in an African context?
options: A) Price based on production cost, competition, and farmer affordability
B) Price at the highest possible amount always
C) Price at zero to beat competitors
D) Price only in foreign currency
quiz.explanation: Balancing cost, market rates, and farmer purchasing power supports sustainable sales.

quiz.q: Which packaging option is practical for smallholder buyers?
options: A) 50-kilogram bags and smaller 10-kilogram packs
B) Only 1-tonne bulk bags
C) Loose piles on the roadside
D) Unlabeled containers
quiz.explanation: Smaller packs suit smallholder budgets and ease of transport, while larger bags serve bigger farms.

quiz.q: What is a key quality control step before selling compost?
options: A) Adding sand to increase weight
B) Testing maturity, nutrient content, and pathogens
C) Mixing in fresh manure
D) Storing in open sunlight forever
quiz.explanation: Testing maturity, nutrients, and pathogens ensures product safety and consistent quality.

quiz.q: Which certification could add value to organic manure in African markets?
options: A) Organic certification from a recognized body
B) A handwritten note
C) No documentation at all
D) A verbal promise only
quiz.explanation: Recognized organic certification builds trust and can open premium markets.

quiz.q: What is a major challenge when scaling compost production?
options: A) Too many customers
B) Consistent supply of quality ingredients and labor
C) Lack of interest from farmers
D) Too much rainfall only
quiz.explanation: Scaling requires reliable ingredient sourcing, trained labor, and consistent production systems.

quiz.q: How can a producer maintain quality while scaling up?
options: A) Skip testing to save time
B) Standardize recipes, train staff, and keep batch records
C) Use random mixtures each time
D) Ignore customer feedback
quiz.explanation: Standardization, training, and record-keeping maintain consistency during growth.

quiz.q: Which reference tool is most useful for a compost entrepreneur in Africa?
options: A) A simple record book and local extension officer contacts
B) A foreign stock market report
C) A fashion magazine
D) A car repair manual
quiz.explanation: Record books and extension officers provide practical, locally relevant support for production and sales.
